evidence.claim: The Horses and Hounds Scenic Byway crosses rolling Maryland countryside, linking horse farms, racecourses and historic estates.
evidence.quote: Drive through the rolling countryside to visit horse farms and experience equestrian events, deeply rooted in Maryland's history.

evidence.claim: Maryland’s tourism office presents the byway as a drive through Hunt Country, where fox hunts and steeplechases remain popular and farms produce Thoroughbreds for major American tracks.
evidence.quote: Located in an area traditionally known as “Hunt Country,” where fox hunts and steeplechase races are still a popular pastime, some of the farms you see during this relaxing drive across the beautiful Maryland countryside are also famous for producing Thoroughbreds that have raced on major tracks across America.

evidence.claim: Historic homes punctuate the rolling fields. The route’s equestrian connections extend from the timber fences of Worthington Valley to Ladew’s sculpted fox hunt and the preserved stable at Hampton.
evidence.quote: a relaxing and scenic drive through rolling countryside dotted with stately historic homes

evidence.claim: Historic homes punctuate the rolling fields.
evidence.quote: rolling, grassy fields

evidence.claim: the timber fences of Worthington Valley
evidence.quote: The Maryland Hunt Cup is four miles long with 22 timber fences. Its permanent home is in Worthington Valley, Maryland.

evidence.claim: the preserved stable at Hampton.
evidence.quote: Tour the main house and visit restored slave quarters and outbuildings, including the 1805 Hampton Stable

evidence.claim: One of its roads had an earlier agricultural purpose: Glen Arm Road formed part of Old Harford Road, carrying farm products from Maryland and southern Pennsylvania toward Baltimore’s port.
evidence.quote: Glen Arm lies along what is now Glen Arm Road, which was once part of Old Harford Road, one of the early routes used for conveying agricultural products from parts of Harford and Baltimore Counties and southern Pennsylvania to the port of Baltimore.

evidence.claim: The equestrian landscape also changed over time. The Maryland Hunt Cup began in 1894 as a contest between two hunt clubs, moving among locations before acquiring a permanent home in Worthington Valley in 1922.
evidence.quote: The Maryland Hunt Cup was established in 1894 as a contest between two hunts, The Elkridge Fox Hunting Club and the Green Spring Fox Hunting Club, to determine the relative merits of the local hunting horses.

evidence.claim: The Maryland Hunt Cup began in 1894 as a contest between two hunt clubs, moving among locations before acquiring a permanent home in Worthington Valley in 1922.
evidence.quote: In 1922, a permanent location for the Maryland Hunt Cup was established in Worthington Valley, where it remains to this day. Prior to this date, the race was run at a variety of locations.

evidence.claim: Start westward from Cockeysville on Shawan Road, then cross Worthington Valley on Tufton Avenue before heading toward Glyndon and Butler.
evidence.quote: The byway begins at I-83 Exit 20 in Cockeysville and heads west along Shawan Road

evidence.claim: Start westward from Cockeysville on Shawan Road, then cross Worthington Valley on Tufton Avenue before heading toward Glyndon and Butler.

evidence.claim: Four miles and 22 timber fences define the Maryland Hunt Cup, whose permanent home is Worthington Valley.
evidence.quote: The Maryland Hunt Cup is four miles long with 22 timber fences. Its permanent home is in Worthington Valley, Maryland.

evidence.claim: The race began in 1894 to compare the hunting horses of the Elkridge and Green Spring clubs. Eligibility widened from those two clubs to Maryland clubs, then to clubs throughout North America in 1903.
evidence.quote: A year later the race was opened up to horses owned and ridden by members of any recognized Hunt Club in Maryland. In 1903 this was further expanded to horses owned and ridden by members of any Hunt Club in North America.

evidence.claim: The race began in 1894 to compare the hunting horses of the Elkridge and Green Spring clubs.
evidence.quote: The Maryland Hunt Cup was established in 1894 as a contest between two hunts, The Elkridge Fox Hunting Club and the Green Spring Fox Hunting Club, to determine the relative merits of the local hunting horses.

evidence.claim: Worthington Valley became the permanent venue in 1922, after the race had moved among several locations during its early years.
evidence.quote: In 1922, a permanent location for the Maryland Hunt Cup was established in Worthington Valley, where it remains to this day. Prior to this date, the race was run at a variety of locations.

evidence.claim: The event remains limited to amateur jockeys. Its solid timber fences imitate the hunt country where many competitors train, bringing that working landscape into the racecourse itself.
evidence.quote: Throughout its history, the Maryland Hunt Cup has been limited to amateur jockeys.

evidence.claim: Its solid timber fences imitate the hunt country where many competitors train, bringing that working landscape into the racecourse itself.
evidence.quote: The Maryland Hunt Cup is a timber race, which is a steeplechase run over solid timber fences. This form of steeplechasing is unique to North America. The timber fences mimic the hunt country over which many of these horses are prepared.

evidence.claim: At Ladew, a fox hunt takes the form of clipped plants: horses, riders, dogs and foxes clear a hedge.
evidence.quote: Ladew designed topiaries depicting a fox hunt with horses, riders, dogs, and foxes clearing a hedge

evidence.claim: Harvey S. Ladew bought a farm in 1929 and established the gardens in the 1930s. His travels in England, where he hunted frequently, strongly influenced the topiary.
evidence.quote: The garden is particularly noted for its topiary, which was strongly influenced by Ladew's extensive travel in England, where he frequently went fox hunting.

evidence.claim: Harvey S. Ladew bought a farm in 1929 and established the gardens in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: The gardens were established in the 1930s by socialite and huntsman Harvey S. Ladew (1887–1976), who in 1929 had bought a 250-acre (100 ha) farm to build his estate.

evidence.claim: The grounds divide into 15 garden rooms devoted to individual colors, plants or themes. Two crossing axes meet at an oval swimming pool, giving the separate rooms an organizing framework. House and gardens opened to the public in 1971.
evidence.quote: The grounds contain 15 garden rooms, each devoted to a single color, plant or theme, arranged around two cross axes with vistas. The axes meet in an oval swimming pool.

evidence.claim: House and gardens opened to the public in 1971.
evidence.quote: Both the grounds and house, which contain a good collection of antique English furniture, opened to the public in 1971.

evidence.claim: Other clipped figures include swans, a giraffe and a Chinese junk complete with sails, extending Ladew’s subjects beyond the hunt.
evidence.quote: a Chinese junk with sails, swans, and a giraffe, among others.

evidence.claim: Look for the fox hunt shaped from topiary, with riders, horses, dogs and foxes clearing a hedge.
evidence.quote: Ladew designed topiaries depicting a fox hunt with horses, riders, dogs, and foxes clearing a hedge

evidence.claim: Hampton’s 1805 stable connects the Ridgely family’s racing interests to the work of free and enslaved Black jockeys and grooms.
evidence.quote: including the 1805 Hampton Stable, where free and enslaved Black men served as jockeys and groomsmen for the Ridgely family.

evidence.claim: The Elkridge Hunt Club met at the estate, and the Maryland Hunt Cup ran through its fields.
evidence.quote: Meets of the Elkridge Hunt Club were held frequently at Hampton and the Maryland Hunt Cup steeplechase was run through Hampton’s fields.

evidence.claim: Under Charles Carnan Ridgely, more than 300 enslaved people worked the fields and household of an estate that also included ironworks, mills and quarries.
evidence.quote: More than 300 enslaved people worked the fields and served the household

evidence.claim: an estate that also included ironworks, mills and quarries.
evidence.quote: The mansion overlooked a grand estate of orchards, ironworks, coal mining, marble quarries, mills, and mercantile interests.

evidence.claim: The preserved estate includes the Georgian mansion, gardens and original stone quarters where enslaved people lived. Those quarters contain exhibits on enslaved life at Hampton; the stone used to build them came from the Ridgelys’ quarry.
evidence.quote: Slave quarters – two preserved stone buildings adjacent to the Farm House, now provided with interpretive exhibits on enslaved life at Hampton. The stone came from the Ridgelys' own stone quarry.

evidence.claim: The preserved estate includes the Georgian mansion, gardens and original stone quarters where enslaved people lived.
evidence.quote: preserves a remnant of a vast 18th-century estate, including a Georgian manor house, gardens, grounds, and the original stone slave quarters.
